title: How to Distill a VLM Into a Small Object Detection Model
summary: VLM distillation: label with Gemini, review in Roboflow, train RF-DETR Nano. The student ran 58x faster than the VLM at 1/43 the cost per image.
body_markdown:
SUMMARY


**To get VLM-quality detections without paying VLM prices on every frame, use a model like Gemini to auto-label your images, correct the labels, and train a small detector to run next to your camera. In Roboflow, you can auto-label with a Gemini Workflow, review in Annotate, train RF-DETR Nano and deploy it with Inference.**


A vision-language model (VLM) can identify cardboard boxes and pallets from a text description. That makes it a useful starting point for building a[warehouse](https://roboflow.com/industries/warehousing?ref=blog.roboflow.com) monitoring application.


For continuous detection, you can use its predictions to train a smaller model that runs on a computer beside the camera, reducing reliance on cloud model calls.


In this guide, I'll build on my[model distillation](https://roboflow.com/blog/model-distillation?ref=blog.roboflow.com) article, where I introduced the teacher-student idea. Here you’ll learn how to distill a VLM into a small object detector with Roboflow. You’ll use Gemini to generate bounding-box annotations, review them in Roboflow Annotate, train an RF-DETR model, and deploy it locally with Roboflow Inference.


[Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean (opens in a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531?ref=blog.roboflow.com) describe how to “compress the knowledge in an ensemble into a single model which is much easier to deploy.” Their method uses soft targets. This tutorial follows the[Autodistill label-generation approach (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.autodistill.com/?ref=blog.roboflow.com#basic-concepts) i.e. teacher predictions become training annotations after human review. It transfers supervision for object detection; it does not transfer the VLM's language capabilities.


I’ll also show you how to evaluate the tradeoffs. You’ll learn how to compare detection quality and inference costs, then measure performance on your own deployment hardware.


**Generate labels with a Gemini teacher, review them, train an RF-DETR student, and deploy the detector at the edge.**


## Step 1: Auto-label with a foundation model


The teacher produces a class and bounding box for each target object. These are candidate annotations: a person will check them before they become student training data.


### 1.1 Create the project and upload images


[Create an Object Detection project (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/datasets/create-and-upload/create-a-project?ref=blog.roboflow.com) , using a name such as. Then[upload the images (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/datasets/create-and-upload/adding-data?ref=blog.roboflow.com) in batches that identify their recording sessions. Preserve the planned training, validation, and test assignments. Use the following annotation rules consistently:


Class Annotation rule


` cardboard box` One bounding box for each identifiable shipping box, not one box around an entire stack.


` pallet` One bounding box for each identifiable pallet, excluding the load above it.


For this example, annotate the visible extent of partially hidden objects. Use the exact same class names throughout labeling, training, and evaluation.


### 1.2 Create and test the Gemini teacher Workflow


[Create a Workflow (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/build/create-a-workflow?ref=blog.roboflow.com) with an image input named` image` and a[Google Gemini v6 block (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/run-a-model/google-gemini?ref=blog.roboflow.com) named` teacher` .


Setting Value


Images` $inputs.image`


Task type` object-detection`


Model` gemini-4-argon` , where available


Classes` cardboard box` ,` pallet`


API key mode` rf_key:account`


Expose` predictions` ,` error_status` ,` input_tokens` , and` output_tokens` from the corresponding outputs of` teacher` . For example, the` predictions` selector is` $steps.teacher.predictions` . The v6 block decodes detection responses itself; no separate conversion block is needed.` error_status=True` means decoding failed and must not be treated as an empty scene.


Save and publish the Workflow as` dispatch-vlm-teacher` .[Test it in the editor (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/build/test-a-workflow?ref=blog.roboflow.com) with a representative image, inspect the boxes and classes, and record the selected Gemini model and saved Workflow ID.


**Gemini teacher Workflow configured to detect cardboard boxes and pallets.**


To test it in the editor, click Run, upload a representative JPG, PNG, or WEBP image, check the selected runtime, and run the Workflow. Inspect the structured` predictions` and` error_status` outputs. The[Workflow testing guide (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/build/test-a-workflow?ref=blog.roboflow.com) explains these controls.


**Testing the Gemini teacher Workflow on a dispatch-area image before auto-labeling the training batch.**


The diagram shows the two inputs and outputs of this teacher. Only the boxes and classes become annotations, the error and token fields help validate the response and measure usage.


**The teacher returns candidate object annotations with error and usage information.**


### 1.3 Generate the training labels


Open the training batch in[Auto Label (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/datasets/annotate/annotate/ai-labeling/auto-label?ref=blog.roboflow.com#label-with-a-workflow) . Select *Workflows* , choose the saved teacher, and map its classes to the project classes. Check the preview and cost estimate, then start *Auto Label With This Workflow* . Unmapped classes are dropped, so confirm both class mappings.


**Using the saved Gemini teacher Workflow in Auto Label to generate training annotations for cardboard boxes and pallets.**


Review a small pilot batch before labeling the full collection. Look for merged stacks, missed pallets, and duplicate boxes. Keep the original teacher output if you want to compare it with the corrected annotations later.


**Other labeling routes:** ** You can choose Gemini directly in Auto Label. If you already use[Autodistill (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.autodistill.com/quickstart/?ref=blog.roboflow.com#how-autodistill-works) , use its Base Model to generate labels and train RF-DETR separately in Step 3. Existing Auto Annotate output can also be imported with its images in a[supported annotation format (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/datasets/create-and-upload/adding-data?ref=blog.roboflow.com) . Each route must provide object boxes and class names; captions alone are insufficient.


## Step 2: Review and fix the labels in Roboflow Annotate


The student learns from the annotations you accept. A missed pallet supplies no positive training example for that object. A box covering an entire stack teaches a different target from a box covering one carton. Review therefore determines what task the student learns.


Open an image in[Roboflow Annotate (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/datasets/annotate/annotate/use-roboflow-annotate?ref=blog.roboflow.com) . Use the selection tool to move boxes or resize their handles, the class editor to change labels, and the bounding box tool to draw missing annotations. Work through each image in this order:


1. *Find missing objects:* Scan the whole image, including borders and partially hidden areas. Do not restrict the review to regions the teacher already found.
2. *Correct class labels:* Apply the class definitions from Step 1.
3. *Correct box boundaries:* Follow the same visible-extent rule throughout the dataset.
4. *Remove incorrect and duplicate boxes:* Each object should contribute one annotation of its class.
5. *Review empty results:* Confirm whether the scene actually lacks the target classes or the teacher missed them.


For example, suppose the teacher finds one of two cardboard boxes and places two overlapping boxes around it. Delete the duplicate, adjust the remaining box, add the missed carton, and check the pallet below them. This is an illustrative correction, not a measured result from the teacher.


**A schematic illustration of teacher predicts the cardboard box class twice for one object and misses the other box and the pallet. Human review removes the duplicate, fixes the boxes, and adds the missing cardboard box and pallet annotations.**


Where Review Mode is available and enabled, use its approval process. Otherwise, still perform the inspection manually. From the annotation job, select the checked images and use *Add N Images to Dataset* . Approval and dataset inclusion are described in[Collaborate on Labeling (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/datasets/annotate/annotate/team-collaboration?ref=blog.roboflow.com) .


Keep a small review log i.e. images checked, missed objects added, incorrect boxes removed, and review minutes. It helps identify a teacher that is inexpensive to call but costly to correct.


## Step 3: Train RF-DETR


The reviewed dataset now represents a two-class detection task. We will train *RF-DETR Nano* , a compact option in the[RF-DETR family (opens in a new tab)](https://rfdetr.roboflow.com/latest/?ref=blog.roboflow.com) , using Roboflow's hosted training flow.


### 3.1 Prepare a dataset version


Open *Versions* and then **** *Generate New Version* . Check the split assignments, select preprocessing and augmentation settings appropriate to the camera scenes, and generate the version. A[dataset version (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/datasets/versions/dataset-versions/create-a-dataset-version?ref=blog.roboflow.com) records the images, annotations, and processing settings used for training.


Preserve the session-based split and confirm that resizing leaves small objects recognizable. Record the version number and image counts.


**Prepared dataset version containing reviewed annotations and the selected training, validation, and test splits.**


### 3.2 Train with Roboflow Custom Training


Use the documented[Custom Training flow (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/models/train/train-a-model?ref=blog.roboflow.com#web-app) :


1. Open *Train* and then **** *Custom Training* .
2. Choose a single architecture, *RF-DETR* , and *Nano* .
3. Select the dataset version prepared above.
4. Review *Customize Training Recipe* , including the checkpoint and hyperparameters. Start from the supported public checkpoint for the first experiment.
5. Review the duration and credit estimate, set a credit cap if appropriate and available, and select *Start Training* .


**Training the student model using Roboflow Auto-Train.**


After training, save the recipe and use[Copy Model ID (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/models/model-ids?ref=blog.roboflow.com) on the resulting model. Multiple training runs can use one dataset version, so copy the actual model ID.


Open the built-in[Training Graphs (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/models/evaluate/training-results?ref=blog.roboflow.com) to inspect the learning curves and object detection metrics. These reports are the first evidence of how training behaved. Use validation examples while deciding whether to change the data or training settings.


**RF-DETR Nano training graphs and detection metrics for the prepared dataset version.**


## Step 4: Deploy at the edge with Roboflow Inference


The trained student can now run on a computer beside the camera. We will create one student Workflow and use it for both a test image and a recorded video. This deployment does not include the Gemini teacher.


### 4.1 Create the student Workflow


Create a Workflow named[rfdetr-student](https://app.roboflow.com/workflows/embed/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ3b3JrZmxvd0lkIjoiMnI0aERJRnJkU2Z1RkxQYUs5aHYiLCJ3b3Jrc3BhY2VJZCI6InZjQmw1Y0x3bUtQallLTGNRemV1VkE4UlRhNjIiLCJ1c2VySWQiOiJ2Y0JsNWNMd21LUGpZS0xjUXpldVZBOFJUYTYyIiwiaWF0IjoxNzk0MjIxMzczfQ.9M-aGQD9FzIy93scqndvCLbrlHkndlMd1E-TGVnyz3E?ref=blog.roboflow.com) with an image input named` image` . Add these built-in blocks:


1. *Object Detection Model* , named` student` : select the trained model ID, connect` $inputs.image` , and set the validation-selected confidence threshold.
2. *Bounding Box Visualization* , named` boxes` : use the input image and` student` predictions.
3. *Label Visualization* , named` labels` : use the image returned by` boxes` and the same` student` predictions.


The[Object Detection Model block (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/run-a-model/object-detection-model?ref=blog.roboflow.com) runs the student. The[visualization blocks (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/build/build-a-workflow?ref=blog.roboflow.com#bounding-box-visualization) draw boxes and class names on one image. Expose these outputs, then save, test, and publish the Workflow:


Output name Selector


` predictions`` $steps.student.predictions`


` output_image`` $steps.labels.image`


**One RF-DETR**[Workflow](https://app.roboflow.com/workflows/embed/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ3b3JrZmxvd0lkIjoiMnI0aERJRnJkU2Z1RkxQYUs5aHYiLCJ3b3Jrc3BhY2VJZCI6InZjQmw1Y0x3bUtQallLTGNRemV1VkE4UlRhNjIiLCJ1c2VySWQiOiJ2Y0JsNWNMd21LUGpZS0xjUXpldVZBOFJUYTYyIiwiaWF0IjoxNzk0MjIxMzczfQ.9M-aGQD9FzIy93scqndvCLbrlHkndlMd1E-TGVnyz3E?ref=blog.roboflow.com) **returns detections and an image annotated with boxes and class labels.**


### 4.2 Start Roboflow Inference on the edge computer


Follow the[device-specific installation guide (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/deployment/self-hosted/inference-server/install?ref=blog.roboflow.com) to prepare Docker and, where applicable, GPU support. On that computer, install the CLI and WebRTC client dependencies, then start the server:


Shell


```text
python   -m   pip   install   inference-cli   "inference-sdk[webrtc]"
inference   server   start
```


The[Inference Server (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/deployment/self-hosted/inference-server?ref=blog.roboflow.com) uses` http://localhost:9001` for local requests. Keep it running while executing the examples. Header authentication in the code requires Inference Server 1.5.0 or newer.


Set your[Roboflow API key (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/reference/authentication/authentication/find-your-roboflow-api-key?ref=blog.roboflow.com) in the terminal that will run the scripts. On Linux or macOS:


Shell


```text
export   ROBOFLOW_API_KEY  =  "YOUR_PRIVATE_API_KEY"
```


On Windows Command Prompt:


Shell


```text
set   ROBOFLOW_API_KEY=YOUR_PRIVATE_API_KEY
```


The first request can download and initialize the model weights. Local execution does not automatically mean disconnected operation; use the separate[Offline Mode guide (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/deployment/self-hosted/enterprise/offline-mode?ref=blog.roboflow.com) if that is a requirement.


### 4.3 Run the Workflow on an image


Place a representative image at` test-image.jpg` . Replace the workspace and saved Workflow IDs below, then save the code as` run_image_workflow.py` . It calls the[Workflow SDK API (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/reference/inference/inference-sdk/workflows?ref=blog.roboflow.com) and prints the detection output.


Python


```text
import   json
import   os
from   inference_sdk   import   InferenceHTTPClient, InferenceConfiguration


client   =   InferenceHTTPClient(
api_url  =  "http://localhost:9001"  ,
api_key  =  os.environ[  "ROBOFLOW_API_KEY"  ],
).configure(InferenceConfiguration(  api_key_transport  =  "header"  ))


results   =   client.run_workflow(
workspace_name  =  "YOUR_WORKSPACE_ID"  ,
workflow_id  =  "YOUR_SAVED_STUDENT_WORKFLOW_ID"  ,
images  =  {  "image"  :   "test-image.jpg"  },
use_cache  =  False  ,
)


for   result   in   results:
print  (json.dumps(result[  "predictions"  ],   indent  =  2  ))
```


Shell


```text
python   run_image_workflow.py
```


The Workflow also returns` output_image` ; the script prints only` predictions` to keep the terminal readable. The editor preview displays the annotated image.` use_cache=False` ensures this verification request uses your updated saved definition.


### 4.4 Run the same Workflow on a video


Place a short warehouse clip at` test-video.mp4` . The built-in[VideoFileSource (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/reference/inference/inference-sdk/webrtc?ref=blog.roboflow.com#videofilesource) sends the file to the local server; the Workflow returns annotated frames and prediction data.


Save this as` run_video_workflow.py` , using the same workspace and Workflow IDs:


Python


```text
import   cv2
import   os
from   inference_sdk   import   InferenceHTTPClient, InferenceConfiguration
from   inference_sdk.webrtc   import   VideoFileSource, StreamConfig


client   =   InferenceHTTPClient(
api_url  =  "http://localhost:9001"  ,
api_key  =  os.environ[  "ROBOFLOW_API_KEY"  ],
).configure(InferenceConfiguration(  api_key_transport  =  "header"  ))


session   =   client.webrtc.stream(
source  =  VideoFileSource(  "test-video.mp4"  ,   realtime_processing  =  False  ),
workflow  =  "YOUR_SAVED_STUDENT_WORKFLOW_ID"  ,
workspace  =  "YOUR_WORKSPACE_ID"  ,
config  =  StreamConfig(
stream_output  =  [  "output_image"  ],
data_output  =  [  "predictions"  ],
realtime_processing  =  False  ,
),
)


@session.on_frame
def   show  (frame, metadata):
cv2.imshow(  "RF-DETR student - press q to stop"  , frame)
if   cv2.waitKey(  1  )   &   0x  FF   ==   ord  (  "q"  ):
session.close()


@session.on_data  (  "predictions"  )
def   report  (predictions, metadata):
print  ({  "frame_id"  : metadata.frame_id,   "predictions"  : predictions})


@session.on_error
def   report_error  (errors, metadata):
print  ({  "frame_id"  : metadata.frame_id,   "errors"  : errors})


try  :
session.run()
finally  :
session.close()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()
```


Shell


```text
python   run_video_workflow.py
```


Run this preview script on the edge computer with a desktop display. Press *q* in the preview window to stop. It uses the Workflow's` output_image` , so the displayed frames include both boxes and class labels. Prediction data appears in the terminal. With real-time processing disabled, this file test is configured to process frames without live-preview pacing; it is a deployment demonstration, not a speed benchmark.


For a camera connected to the same computer, import` WebcamSource` and replace the source with` WebcamSource()` . Use` realtime_processing=True` in` StreamConfig` for a live preview. See the[video Workflow guide (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/deploy/video-processing?ref=blog.roboflow.com) for source options.


## Benchmark the student against the teacher: accuracy, FPS, cost per image


The final check is whether the student meets the application's needs. Check three things:


- whether the student detects the required objects correctly,
- how quickly it processes inputs, and
- what inference costs.


For a direct teacher–student comparison, use the same held-out images, class definitions, and comparable Workflow settings.


### Accuracy: compare detections with Workflow Evals


Accuracy evaluation checks the predicted classes and bounding boxes against independently reviewed reference labels. Missed objects and false detections both matter. Use[Workflow Evals (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/evaluate/workflow-evals?ref=blog.roboflow.com) as follows:


1. Open *Workflows* -> *Evals* -> *Create Eval* in your workspace.
2. Choose the Workflow. Use the server selector to choose where it runs.
3. Import your held-out images from a Dataset test set, the Asset Library, or your device. Select` predictions` as the output to evaluate.
4. Review the reference annotations, correcting missing boxes, incorrect classes, and box boundaries. Approve each Case with *Add to Ground Truth* . Imported labels require review before approval.
5. Add an object-detection Check and set its thresholds. Use *Run preview* to verify the Check on one Case.
6. Review the configuration and credit estimate, then start the evaluation. Evaluate both teacher and student against the same Cases and Checks.
7. Open *Metrics* to compare the detection results and inspect failing Cases. Report the metric name and aggregation used; a Check pass rate is different from detection accuracy.


### FPS and latency: measure processing performance


Latency is the time taken to return a result; throughput is the number of requests or images processed per second. For video, FPS describes the measured number of frames processed per second.


For cloud measurements, use *Benchmark Workflow* in the saved Workflow's toolbar:


1. Select the image set, deployment service, and request load.
2. Run the benchmark and record its throughput, latency percentiles, and failed requests.
3. Repeat for the other Workflow. For a direct comparison, keep the images, service, request rate, duration, and warm-up settings the same, with comparable visualization and other processing blocks.


**Open Benchmark Workflow from the saved student Workflow to measure cloud performance and billed cost.**


The completed reports below both used *Cloud API* , a configured load of **1** *request/second* , and *120 planned inferences over 2 minutes* . The student report showed *409 ms median latency* and *1,062 ms p95 latency* ; the teacher report showed *23.8 s median latency* and *58.4 s p95 latency* . The p95 value means approximately 95% of measured requests completed within that time.


Both Workflows used *all 100 images in Pallet Monitoring* . The results therefore cover the same image set and configured request load. They describe the complete Workflows under these cloud test conditions.


Throughput was *0.96 requests/second* for the student and *0.72* **** *requests/second* for the teacher under the configured one-request-per-second load. The teacher report flagged that it delivered *72% of the configured request rate* and did not fully keep up with this load. It recorded *two failed requests* across the whole run, compared with *zero* for the student. These numbers describe Cloud API Workflow requests rather than isolated model inference or edge-device video FPS. A test configured for one request per second does not establish the student's maximum processing rate.


To measure the student on the target edge device, use the[built-in Inference benchmark (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/reference/inference/inference-cli/benchmark?ref=blog.roboflow.com) :


1. Start the Inference Server on the edge computer, using the deployment setup in Step 4.
2. Follow the API benchmark example in the linked guide, supplying the trained model ID, representative test-image directory, and report output directory.
3. Review the saved throughput, latency, errors, and platform details. Record the hardware and request settings, and identify whether timing covers a model endpoint or a complete Workflow.


Report an image benchmark as *images/second* . For video, measure processed frames per second over a stated interval and identify whether network transfer and visualization are included. Keep the video input rate separate from the processing rate.


### Cost per image: use the billed benchmark report


The Cost Benchmark report displayed *5.19 credits per 1,000 inferences* for the teacher and *0.12 credits per 1,000 inferences* for the student. These correspond to approximately *0.0052* and *0.00012 credits per inference* , respectively. For requests containing one image, they are also the displayed costs per image. These are the displayed rounded rates for the two Workflows on the Pallet Monitoring image set.


The teacher report attributed its measured cost to *Workflows (3rd Party Blocks)* ; the student report showed *Cloud API* charges. For additional attribution, use[Credit Usage and its audit log (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/platform/billing-and-plans/credits/view-credit-usage?ref=blog.roboflow.com) , filtering by the experiment's time window and API key or folder.


Warm-up traffic is billed but excluded from the reports' steady-window rates, latency, and throughput. *Total Billed* covers the whole run, so keep it separate from normalized cost per inference. For edge deployment, state any hardware and electricity allocation separately. Keep auto-labeling, annotation review, and training costs separate from deployed inference.

## Conclusion


Build a detector for your camera footage by starting with an[Object Detection project in Roboflow](https://app.roboflow.com/?ref=blog.roboflow.com) . Upload a small, representative set of images, use a Gemini teacher to generate annotations, and review the boxes before training your first RF-DETR model.


From there, use Roboflow Workflows to test the detector on new images and Roboflow Inference to run it on compatible edge hardware. Check missed objects, processing speed, and operating costs to decide what to improve before expanding the deployment.


[Get started in Roboflow](https://app.roboflow.com/?ref=blog.roboflow.com) by uploading your first batch of images and previewing the teacher’s annotations.
